en: Gajakesari Yoga
Jupiter is placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) counted from the Moon.
Classically associated with intelligence, eloquence, good reputation, prosperity, and respect in society; the native is often remembered fondly and finds success in dealing with others.
It is one of the most widely cited benefic yogas in popular and classical literature alike.

Effects are considerably weaker if Jupiter is debilitated, combust (too close to the Sun), or placed in a dusthana (6th, 8th, or 12th) from the lagna; the yoga is strongest when Jupiter is additionally well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well-aspected).
Ruchaka Yoga (Panch Mahapurusha)
Mars occupies its own sign (Aries or Scorpio) or its exaltation sign (Capricorn), while also being placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the lagna.

Grants a strong, athletic physique, courageous and commanding personality, natural leadership, and success in fields requiring decisive action such as the military, sports, engineering, or entrepreneurship.
The native is typically direct, energetic, and unafraid of competition.
Full strength requires Mars to be free of heavy affliction; the yoga is considered most powerful when Mars is also well-aspected by benefics or otherwise unafflicted.
Bhadra Yoga (Panch Mahapurusha)
Mercury occupies its own sign (Gemini or Virgo) or its exaltation sign (Virgo), while also being placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the lagna.
Grants exceptional intelligence, eloquence, and business or analytical acumen, with natural skill in communication, trade, writing, or scholarship.
The native is typically quick-witted, versatile, and well-regarded for their intellect.
Effects are strongest when Mercury is also unafflicted by malefic conjunction or aspect, and further supported by a strong Mercury dasha period.
Hamsa Yoga (Panch Mahapurusha)
Jupiter occupies its own sign (Sagittarius or Pisces) or its exaltation sign (Cancer), while also being placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the lagna.
Grants wisdom, righteousness, and a dignified, respected character, often producing a natural teacher, counselor, or spiritually inclined figure of good repute.
The native's conduct tends to be principled and their fortune generally favorable.
Most powerful when Jupiter is also unafflicted and well-aspected; a Jupiter under heavy malefic influence will express this yoga's virtues less fully.
Malavya Yoga (Panch Mahapurusha)
Venus occupies its own sign (Taurus or Libra) or its exaltation sign (Pisces), while also being placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the lagna.
Grants charm, artistic or aesthetic talent, a comfortable and often luxurious lifestyle, and harmonious personal relationships.
The native tends to be attractive in manner or appearance and drawn toward refined, pleasurable pursuits.
Full expression depends on Venus being free of significant affliction; a well-aspected Venus in this yoga particularly favors the arts, luxury goods, or diplomacy as career paths.
Sasa Yoga (Panch Mahapurusha)
Saturn occupies its own sign (Capricorn or Aquarius) or its exaltation sign (Libra), while also being placed in a kendra (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th house) from the lagna.
Grants disciplined authority, leadership ability (especially over large groups, institutions, or the working masses), and long-term success achieved through sustained, patient effort.
The native often rises to a position of responsibility later in life through genuine, earned merit.
Strongest when Saturn is not heavily afflicted; because Saturn's own nature favors delay, results under this yoga still tend to arrive gradually rather than early.
Kendra-Trikona Raja Yoga
The lord of a kendra house (1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th) forms a connection — by conjunction, mutual aspect, or exchange of signs (parivartana) — with the lord of a trikona house (1st, 5th, or 9th).
Since the 1st house is both kendra and trikona, any strong connection involving the lagna lord is especially significant.
Considered one of the most important categories of yoga for worldly status, authority, wealth, and rising fortune in Parashari astrology.
The native typically experiences a marked rise in position, especially during the dashas of the planets involved.

The strength of the resulting rise depends heavily on the dignity (sign strength) of the participating lords and the houses they occupy; a Raja Yoga formed by well-placed, unafflicted lords in good houses produces far more pronounced results than one formed by weak or afflicted lords.
Dhana Yoga (2nd-11th Lord Wealth Combination)

PINNED PRIMARY DEFINITION for this dataset: the lord of the 2nd house (dhana, wealth) and the lord of the 11th house (labha, gains) form a connection with each other — by mutual conjunction, mutual aspect, or exchange of signs (parivartana).

Classical and popular sources do not converge on one single fixed configuration for 'Dhana Yoga' (unlike, say, the tightly-defined Pancha Mahapurusha yogas), so this 2nd-11th lord connection was deliberately selected as the dataset's default because it is the single most consistently cited 'core' formulation across sources.

A commonly recognized EXTENDED form also exists: the 2nd or 11th lord additionally connecting with a trikona lord (5th or 9th), or a natural benefic occupying or aspecting the 2nd or 11th house — these are treated here as secondary/extended variants rather than the core definition, and are noted separately where relevant.

Indicates the potential for financial prosperity and accumulation of wealth, activating most strongly during the dasha periods of the 2nd and 11th lords (or, for the extended variant, the additional trikona lord or benefic involved).
Multiple distinct dhana yogas present together in one chart compound and reinforce the overall wealth potential.

A dhana yoga formed by lords of dusthana houses (6th, 8th, or 12th) sharing this connection, or afflicted by malefics without other support, produces a weaker or more complicated form of wealth (e.g. wealth through struggle, litigation, or with ethical compromise) rather than clean prosperity.

If your primary reference text defines Dhana Yoga differently, treat the pinned definition above as this dataset's default and adjust as needed — it was a deliberate editorial choice among several valid classical framings, not a uniquely 'correct' one.
Kemadruma Yoga

No planet other than Rahu/Ketu occupies the 2nd or 12th house from the Moon, and the Moon receives no conjunction or supporting aspect from any other planet (nodes excluded from this count too) — leaving the Moon effectively isolated in the chart.
Classically associated with instability, struggle, lack of consistent support from others, or a sense of emotional isolation, particularly in earlier life.
This is one of the more feared combinations in popular astrology.

Classical texts list numerous cancellation (Bhanga) conditions that are frequently overlooked in casual analysis, including: the Moon placed in a kendra (1st/4th/7th/10th) from the lagna; the Moon receiving aspect from a benefic (e.g. Jupiter or Venus); a benefic occupying a kendra from the Moon; the Moon posited in Taurus or Cancer (both considered to significantly weaken the yoga); or a strong lagna lord/benefics in kendra from the ascendant providing resilience.

Any single one of these is generally enough to substantially reduce or cancel the yoga, so a genuinely uncancelled Kemadruma is less common than its popular reputation suggests, and a full check for these conditions should always precede any negative interpretation.
Neecha Bhanga Raja Yoga

A planet's debilitation (neecha) is cancelled under specific classical conditions — commonly cited variants include: the lord of the debilitation sign itself occupies a kendra from the lagna or the Moon; the planet that would be exalted in the debilitated planet's sign is placed in a kendra from the lagna or Moon; the debilitated planet is otherwise strengthened through conjunction or aspect with its dispositor or exaltation-sign lord under favorable placement rules; or the debilitated planet occupies its own sign or exaltation sign in the Navamsa (D9) chart even while debilitated in the main chart (D1).
Classical texts (e.g. Phaladeepika) enumerate several such rules, and not all schools weight them identically.

When genuinely cancelled, the planet's apparent weakness reverses into a source of significant strength and good fortune — often associated with a dramatic rise from early adversity, hardship, or obscurity to notable, self-made success later in life.

The cancellation is considered strongest ('cleanest') — and most likely to produce a true Raja Yoga rather than mere neutralization of the weakness — when multiple confirming conditions are present simultaneously, and when the planets involved additionally hold kendra or trikona lordship; a marginal or single-condition cancellation produces a milder version of the reversal.
Vipreet Raja Yoga - Harsha
The lord of the 6th house is placed in the 6th, 8th, or 12th house.

Placement in the 6th lord's own house (a 'self-placement' variant) is accepted by many traditions, though placement in a DIFFERENT dusthana (8th or, especially, 12th — read as 'loss of enemies') is generally considered the stronger, more classical form of the yoga.

A dusthana lord placed among the dusthanas is classically read as two difficulties neutralizing each other, producing an unexpected reversal: protection from enemies, litigation, and disease, along with resilience and gains connected to overcoming competition or obstacles.

Some classical commentators note the yoga can be diluted ('spoiled') if the 6th lord additionally receives a strong connection with kendra or trikona lords or benefics, since this ties the dusthana lord too closely to auspicious houses; this point is debated across traditions, as is the relative strength of the self-placement (6th-in-6th) variant versus cross-dusthana placement.
See also the generic house_lord_placement entries where lord_of_house is 6 and placed_in_house is 6, 8, or 12.
Vipreet Raja Yoga - Sarala
The lord of the 8th house is placed in the 6th, 8th, or 12th house.

Placement in the 8th lord's own house (a 'self-placement' variant, associated with unusual composure navigating sudden events) is accepted by some traditions, though placement in a DIFFERENT dusthana (6th or 12th) is generally considered the stronger, more classical form of the yoga.
Classically associated with courage in the face of danger, resilience against sudden misfortune, and an unexpected capacity to convert crisis into strength.
The native often shows notable composure when facing life's difficult transitions.

As with the other Vipareeta Raja Yogas, some commentators note the effect can be diluted if the 8th lord is also strongly connected to kendra/trikona lords or benefics; a 'purer' dusthana-to-DIFFERENT-dusthana placement is considered to produce the fullest reversal effect, versus the milder self-placement variant.
Vipreet Raja Yoga - Vimala
The lord of the 12th house is placed in the 6th, 8th, or 12th house.

Placement in the 12th lord's own house (a 'self-placement' variant, associated with expenditure staying under control) is accepted by some traditions, though placement in a DIFFERENT dusthana (6th or 8th) is generally considered the stronger, more classical form of the yoga.

Classically associated with contentment despite limited material means, ethical restraint regarding expenditure and loss, and an unexpected capacity to find security or spiritual benefit precisely where loss might otherwise be expected.

As with the other Vipareeta Raja Yogas, the reversal is considered strongest when the 12th lord is not simultaneously drawn into a strong kendra/trikona connection, and when it lands in a different dusthana rather than its own; opinions on both points vary by classical school.
Chandra-Mangal Yoga
The Moon and Mars are conjunct in the same house.
Classically associated with enterprising drive, strong business or entrepreneurial acumen, and the capacity to generate wealth through sustained personal effort, real estate, or dynamic ventures.
The combination blends emotional intensity with energetic initiative.

Depending on other chart factors, the same intensity can also manifest as emotional volatility, a quick temper, or impulsive financial decisions if Mars and the Moon are otherwise afflicted; the yoga's wealth-generating potential is strongest when both planets are reasonably well-placed by sign.
Guru-Mangal Yoga
Jupiter and Mars are conjunct in the same house, or placed in mutual kendra aspect to each other.

Combines Jupiter's wisdom and ethical orientation with Mars's courage and drive, favoring leadership in fields that require both principled judgment and decisive action, such as law, defense, medicine, or entrepreneurship.
The native often shows conviction backed by genuine capability.
Results are most favorable when neither planet is significantly afflicted; a heavily afflicted combination can instead produce dogmatic or overly aggressive assertion of one's beliefs.
Amala Yoga
A natural benefic planet (Jupiter, Venus, a well-placed Mercury, or a waxing Moon) occupies the 10th house counted from the lagna or from the Moon, without affliction from malefics.

The name means 'spotless' or 'pure,' and the yoga is classically associated with a lasting, untarnished reputation, ethical conduct in public and professional life, philanthropy, and a benevolent influence that others remember well.
The benefic quality of the placement is essential; if the 10th house benefic is heavily afflicted by malefic conjunction or aspect, the purity implied by this yoga is correspondingly reduced.
Adhi Yoga

Natural benefic planets (Jupiter, Venus, and/or Mercury) occupy the 6th, 7th, and 8th houses counted from the Moon (Chandra-Adhi Yoga, the classical default), whether individually spread across these houses or in combination.
Some traditions also recognize a Lagna-Adhi variant using the same 6th/7th/8th houses counted from the ascendant instead of the Moon.

Traditionally associated with a comfortable, prosperous, and influential life, often linked in classical texts with ministerial-level or high administrative status, along with protection from enemies, obstacles, and misfortune.
The yoga is considered stronger the more of the three houses (6th, 7th, and 8th from the Moon) are occupied by benefics, and stronger still when those benefics are themselves well-dignified.
Shakat Yoga
The Moon is placed in the 6th, 8th, or 12th house counted from Jupiter (equivalently, Jupiter is not in a kendra relationship to the Moon).
Classically associated with fluctuating fortune — periods of prosperity alternating with periods of hardship or setback, particularly regarding status, finances, or emotional stability.

This is a fairly commonly occurring configuration, and many classical commentators note its severity depends heavily on the underlying strength of the Moon and Jupiter and on other supporting or mitigating yogas present in the chart, rather than indicating uniform hardship on its own.
Kalasarpa Yoga
All seven classical planets (Sun through Saturn) are positioned within the 180-degree arc running from Rahu to Ketu on one side of the chart, with none of them crossing to the other side.

In popular modern practice, this configuration is widely associated with obstacles, delays, a sense of being constrained by fate or inherited (ancestral) karma, and a generally more difficult path to achieving one's goals.

It is worth noting for verification purposes that this yoga's popular framework is not extensively documented in the way it is discussed today within the oldest core classical texts (such as BPHS); several researchers who have reviewed the classical corpus note it appears to be a later (possibly medieval-era) addition rather than an ancient one.

It should also be distinguished from the classically-attested 'Sarpa Dosha' (a related but distinct affliction involving Rahu/Ketu that IS discussed in older sources) with which it is sometimes conflated in popular usage.

Many serious practitioners treat Kalasarpa Yoga itself with caution, evaluate it based on which specific houses Rahu and Ketu occupy, and weigh it alongside the chart's overall strength rather than as a standalone, uniformly negative indicator.
Grahan Yoga (Sun/Moon with Rahu-Ketu)
The Sun or the Moon is conjunct Rahu or Ketu in the same house (an 'eclipse-type' combination).

Classically understood as the node 'eclipsing' or obscuring the luminary's natural significations — a Sun-node conjunction can affect vitality, relationship with the father, self-confidence, or standing with authority; a Moon-node conjunction can affect emotional stability, the mind, or relationship with the mother.
Effects are considered particularly active during the dasha periods of the planets involved.

Some traditions distinguish Sun-Rahu/Moon-Rahu (often read as amplifying and obsessive) from Sun-Ketu/Moon-Ketu (often read as detaching and destabilizing) rather than treating all four combinations identically; house placement and sign strongly modify the specific area of life affected.
Angarak Yoga
Mars is conjunct Rahu in the same house.

Classically associated with amplified aggression, impulsiveness, and conflict-prone tendencies, and often linked with heightened risk of accidents, disputes, litigation, or blood-related health matters in the house or life area involved.

When the underlying chart is otherwise strong and well-supported, the same intensified energy can instead express as unusual courage, competitive drive, or willingness to pursue high-risk, high-reward ventures constructively.

Mars is placed in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th, or 12th house from the lagna (specific lists of houses vary slightly by classical school, and some traditions also check Mars's placement from the Moon and from Venus for a fuller assessment).

Traditionally examined specifically in the context of marriage compatibility (kundali matching), and associated with potential friction, delay, or discord affecting marital harmony or the spouse's wellbeing.

Classical texts provide numerous cancellation (Dosha Bhanga) conditions that are essential to check before drawing conclusions — for example, when both prospective partners carry a matching Kuja Dosha (which cancels in most traditions), when Mars occupies its own or exalted sign, or when Mars receives supportive aspects or conjunctions from certain benefics.
A raw placement check without these cancellations is considered an incomplete assessment.
Guru Chandal Yoga
Jupiter is conjunct Rahu (and, in some interpretive traditions, conjunct Ketu) in the same house.

Classically associated with a clouding or distortion of Jupiter's natural wisdom, ethical clarity, and guidance-oriented significations, sometimes linked with unconventional belief systems, controversial teacher or mentor figures, or ethically ambiguous decision-making in the area of life involved.

The same combination can, depending on the rest of the chart, indicate unusually innovative or unconventional wisdom and teaching ability that constructively breaks from tradition rather than purely negative distortion — the outcome depends significantly on Jupiter's dignity and other supporting factors.
Saturn is conjunct Rahu in the same house (literally the 'poison combination').

Associated with a corrosive, undermining quality affecting the significations of the house involved, often manifesting as prolonged obstacles, chronic difficulties, or slow-burning conflicts in that area of life rather than sudden, dramatic events.

House and sign placement strongly shape which specific life area is most affected, and a careful, house-specific assessment is recommended rather than a blanket negative prediction whenever this combination is found.

A combust Moon is considered one of the more significant combustion effects: the mind, emotional steadiness, and sense of security can feel destabilized or overshadowed, since the Moon's own light is what the Sun's proximity is overwhelming most directly.
Classically associated with a restless or anxious disposition until the Moon separates from the Sun.
A combust Mars can show as suppressed drive or courage that surfaces in bursts rather than steady application - initiative that's present but doesn't get a clean, sustained outlet.
Some texts note it can also manifest as impulsiveness when the pent-up energy does release.
A combust Mercury is one of the more common combustion placements (Mercury is never more than about 28 degrees from the Sun by definition, so close conjunctions happen often).
Effects are usually read as mildly clouded or hesitant communication and decision-making rather than a severe affliction - intellect present but not shining as clearly as it otherwise would.
A combust Jupiter can dampen the confidence, optimism, and sound judgment Jupiter usually lends, along with the areas it governs for this chart (wisdom, higher learning, fortune, teachers).
Read as the Sun's ego/authority theme temporarily overshadowing Jupiter's own expansive, guiding nature.

A combust Venus is often read as affecting comfort in relationships, aesthetic expression, or material pleasures - a sense that these areas are present but muted or complicated, rather than flowing easily.
Some texts specifically note friction in romantic or partnership matters.

A combust Saturn can intensify Saturn's already-serious themes (discipline, delay, responsibility) into something closer to real hardship or heaviness, since Saturn's own slow, structural nature isn't well suited to being overwhelmed by the Sun's fast, ego-driven light.
Some texts read this combination as particularly challenging.

marriage, dharma, overall strength

Considered the second most important chart after the main birth chart (Rasi/D1), the Navamsa is used to assess the strength of a planet's true underlying nature, the quality and timing of marriage, the spouse's characteristics, and the native's inner dharmic disposition.
A planet occupying the same sign in both D1 and D9 is called Vargottama, a condition that significantly reinforces that planet's strength and reliability of results.

Navamsa divisions are assigned to signs following a fixed classical starting-sign scheme based on the element (fire/earth/air/water) of the birth sign; the resulting D9 sign for a given birth-chart degree should be computed with a verified calculation method or ephemeris library rather than derived manually in the app.
career, profession
Used specifically to assess career direction, professional status, public achievement, and the general trajectory of the native's working life.
Planets and house lords are examined in the D10 much as in the main chart, but with the questions reframed specifically around profession, authority, and public standing.

The starting sign for the ten divisions alternates by odd/even birth sign per classical rule; as with all vargas, exact division boundaries should be computed programmatically from precise birth data rather than approximated.
parents, lineage

Used to examine matters relating to parents in more depth than the main chart's 4th (mother) and 9th (father) houses alone, including ancestral heritage, family lineage patterns, and the native's inherited circumstances.
The twelve divisions of a sign map onto the twelve signs of the zodiac in fixed forward order starting from the birth sign itself.
siblings, courage

Used to examine siblings (particularly the nature of the relationship with them) and the native's courage, valor, and capacity for self-initiated effort in more depth than the main chart's 3rd house alone provides.

The three divisions of a sign are classically assigned to the sign itself, the 5th sign from it, and the 9th sign from it (a trikona-based scheme), though some later systems use alternate assignment rules.
property, fortune
Used to examine matters of property, fixed assets, homes, and general fortune or luck in more depth than the main chart's 4th house alone provides.
The four divisions of a sign are classically assigned to the sign itself and the 4th, 7th, and 10th signs from it (a kendra-based scheme).
wealth
Used to examine wealth and financial resources specifically, refining the main chart's 2nd and 11th house indications.

Each half of a sign is classically assigned to either the Sun or the Moon (via their traditional rulership of Leo and Cancer), depending on whether the sign is odd or even and which half of the sign is involved.
The exact Sun/Moon assignment rule differs slightly for odd versus even signs and should be implemented per the classical formula rather than approximated.
education, learning
Used to examine formal and informal education, academic achievement, and the depth of learning or mastery (siddhi) the native attains in various fields of knowledge.
The starting sign for the twenty-four divisions depends on whether the birth sign is odd or even, following a fixed classical rule.
vehicles, comforts
Used to examine vehicles, general material comforts, and overall quality-of-life pleasures beyond the essentials, refining themes touched on by the main chart's 4th house.
The starting sign for the sixteen divisions follows a fixed classical rule based on the movable/fixed/dual nature (modality) of the birth sign.
spiritual pursuits
Used to examine spiritual inclination, religious or devotional practice, and the native's capacity for and progress toward initiation into a spiritual path or discipline.
The starting sign for the twenty divisions follows a fixed classical rule based on the modality (movable/fixed/dual) of the birth sign.
misfortunes, weaknesses

Used to examine vulnerabilities, misfortunes, moral or characterological weaknesses, and areas where the native may be prone to difficulty or poor judgment, complementing the generally more fortune-oriented focus of most other divisional charts.

Because the five planetary divisions within each sign have unequal degree spans (unlike the other vargas listed here, which divide each sign into equal parts) and the assignment order differs for odd versus even signs, this chart requires particularly careful, rule-verified implementation.
past-life karma, fine-grained results

Considered by many classical authorities (including Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra) to be the single most sensitive and important divisional chart for fine-grained confirmation of results and for understanding past-life karma (purva janma) carried into the current birth.
Because of its extremely fine 0.5-degree resolution, it is highly sensitive to birth time accuracy.

Given the 0.5-degree resolution, an accurate birth time (ideally verified/rectified) is essential; small birth-time errors of only a minute or two can shift the D60 sign, so this chart's reliability depends more heavily on precise input data than any other varga listed here.

The Ashwini Kumaras (twin divine physician-horsemen)
A horse's head
The zodiac's first nakshatra, and it behaves like one: quick to start, quick to heal, impatient for results.
The Ashwini Kumaras are the gods' physicians, so there's a natural gift for fast, practical remedies — fixing what's broken and moving on before it's fully understood.
The horse-head symbol fits: forward motion, a burst of energy rather than a sustained one.
Yama (god of death, judgment, and dharma)
The yoni (womb) — a triangle
Bharani carries the weight Ashwini's burst of energy doesn't have to: seeing a difficult, often transformative process all the way through, under Yama's watch rather than by impulse.
Fertility, endurance, and a strong (sometimes severe) internal sense of right and wrong all sit here — creative or generative power that insists on being earned.
Agni (god of fire)
A razor or a flame
Agni's fire both purifies and cuts, and Krittika does both: a sharp, sometimes blunt clarity that separates what's useful from what isn't.
Nurturing (the symbol is also linked to the Pleiades, the 'six nurses' who raised the war-god Skanda), but nurturing that doesn't flinch from honest criticism.
Brahma (or, in some tellings, Prajapati) / presided over by growth itself
An ox-cart, or a sprouting shoot

Classically the Moon's favorite wife among the 27 nakshatra-consorts, and the association fits: Rohini is about things ripening — beauty, sensual pleasure, land, and material comfort that grows steadily rather than arrives suddenly.
A magnetic, aesthetically-inclined nakshatra with a strong pull toward stability once it takes root.
Soma (the Moon, as a nourishing deity)
A deer's head
The deer-head symbol is literal: always turned slightly further, sensing something not quite in view yet.
Mrigashira natives tend toward restless, exploratory curiosity — happiest mid-search, and prone to losing interest once a thing is actually caught.
Gentle rather than forceful in how it pursues.
Rudra (the fierce storm-form of Shiva)
A teardrop, or a diamond
Rudra's domain, and it reads that way: a nakshatra of storms that clear rather than merely destroy.
Ardra often correlates with periods of real upheaval — grief, breakdown, sharp change — that, classically, are the necessary weather before genuine renewal.
Intense, sometimes turbulent, rarely gentle about it.
Aditi (mother of the gods, goddess of boundlessness)
A bow and quiver, or a house
The name literally means 'return of the light' — after Ardra's storm, a homecoming.
Aditi's boundless, unconditionally nurturing nature colors this nakshatra with resilience and optimism: whatever was lost or scattered can be gathered again.
A restorative, safety-making energy, good at starting over without bitterness.
Brihaspati (Jupiter, guru of the gods)
A cow's udder, a lotus, or an arrow
Widely held as the single most auspicious nakshatra for undertakings of real consequence, under the guru-planet's own guidance.
Pushya nourishes — literally (the udder symbol), and through steady, disciplined care rather than dramatic gesture.
A dependable, protective, quietly authoritative energy.
The Nagas (serpent deities)
A coiled serpent
Serpent symbolism throughout: a sharp, perceptive, sometimes unsettling intelligence that can coil close and hold on.

Ashlesha's gift is the same faculty that can heal (classical medicine's association with serpents/venom-as-remedy) or harm — penetrating insight used well or used to manipulate, with the nakshatra itself agnostic about which.
The Pitris (ancestors)
A royal throne, or a palanquin
Magha means 'the mighty one,' and its rulership by the ancestors gives it a strong pull toward legacy — position, inheritance, and a felt duty to those who came before.
A regal, lineage-conscious nakshatra: comfortable with authority, and inclined to measure success partly by what it passes on.
Bhaga (god of fortune and marital bliss)
The front legs of a bed, or a hammock
Under Bhaga's rulership this is a nakshatra of enjoyed reward: romance, creative pleasure, and a genuine talent for rest that isn't idleness so much as recovery.
Warm, sociable, drawn toward beauty and comfort — the part of the cycle that gets to enjoy what's been earned.
Aryaman (god of patronage, contracts, and favorable unions)
The back legs of a bed, or a small cot
Where Purva Phalguni enjoys, Uttara Phalguni extends that generosity outward: helpful partnership, fair contracts, and a steady, patron-like kindness.
Aryaman is also the deity most associated with marriage in its social/contractual sense — reliability and follow-through in commitments made to others.
Savitar (a solar deity, patron of skillful action)
A hand, or a closed fist
The hand symbol says it plainly: Hasta is about making things happen through skilled, practical action, not abstraction.
Craftsmanship, manual dexterity, and a talent for 'getting the job done' with whatever's actually available.
A grounded, capable, results-oriented energy.
Tvashtar / Vishwakarma (the divine architect and craftsman)
A bright jewel, or a pearl
Named for brilliance ('the bright one'), and ruled by the gods' own master-builder — Chitra combines Hasta's practical skill with a strong aesthetic and charismatic sense of design.
Good at making something that stands out: striking, well-crafted, and hard to look away from.
Vayu (god of wind)
A young shoot bending in the wind, or coral
Vayu's domain is movement without a fixed path, and Swati carries that: independence, adaptability, and a preference for self-direction over instruction.
Flexible rather than rigid — like the young shoot in the symbol, it bends with pressure instead of breaking, and keeps moving on its own terms.
Indra and Agni (jointly)
A triumphal archway, or a potter's wheel

The name means 'forked branch,' and the dual rulership (Indra's ambition, Agni's drive) fits a nakshatra defined by determined, sometimes single-minded pursuit of a goal — with a real choice-point along the way about which branch to commit to.
Driven, competitive, and effective once the fork is resolved.
Mitra (god of friendship and alliance)
A lotus flower, or a triumphal archway
Mitra rules alliance itself, and Anuradha reflects it: success that comes through cooperation, loyalty, and disciplined devotion to a shared goal or person rather than solo ambition.
Warm and relationship-oriented, with real staying power once committed.
Indra (king of the gods)
A circular amulet, an umbrella, or an earring

The name means 'the eldest/most senior,' and under Indra's kingly rulership this nakshatra carries real authority — along with the isolation and responsibility that often comes with being the one others lean on.
Protective, capable of command, but prone to feeling the weight of that position.
Nirriti (goddess of destruction and dissolution)
A bunch of roots, or a lion's tail
Mula literally means 'root,' and Nirriti's rulership makes this a nakshatra of getting to the bottom of things — sometimes by tearing down what's built on a false foundation first.
Investigative, unafraid of destruction when it's in service of finding what's actually true underneath.
Apas (goddess of the cosmic waters)
An elephant's tusk, or a fan/winnowing basket
The name means 'the early/invincible one,' and Apas's water rulership gives it a purifying, unstoppable-early-momentum quality — conviction that clears obstacles the way water wears down stone.
Strong-willed, persuasive, and quick to gain ground once committed to a direction.
The Vishvadevas (the universal/all-gods)
An elephant's tusk, or the back legs of a small bed

Where Purva Ashadha is early and forceful, Uttara Ashadha is the victory that lasts — earned slowly, through integrity, and recognized broadly (the universal-gods rulership) rather than won by force alone.
Principled, patient, and durable in what it achieves.
Vishnu
An ear, or three footprints

The name means 'hearing,' and the ear symbol is direct: this is a nakshatra of learning by listening — to teachers, to tradition, to what others have to say — and of connecting people through communication.
Under Vishnu's preserving rulership, it favors continuity: passing knowledge on rather than inventing from scratch.
The eight Vasus (gods of the elements and material wealth)
A drum, or a flute
The Vasus rule material abundance, and Dhanishta channels it through rhythm and shared celebration — music, group recognition, and a prosperity that's often public rather than private.
Adaptable and socially attuned, with a real talent for timing.
Varuna (god of the cosmic waters and cosmic law)
An empty circle, or a hundred stars/flowers

The name means 'a hundred physicians,' and Varuna's rulership over the unseen deep gives this nakshatra a secretive, investigative healing quality — comfortable working alone, drawn to what's hidden or not yet understood, and skeptical of anything too easily explained.
Aja Ekapada (the one-footed goat/serpent, a fierce form of Rudra)
A funeral cot's front legs, or a two-edged sword
A fierce, intense nakshatra under a fierce, intense deity — spiritual or psychological transformation that comes through burning away what's false rather than gentle unlearning.
Passionate, penetrating, sometimes uncomfortable to be near, but genuinely purifying in effect.
Ahir Budhnya (the serpent of the deep)
A funeral cot's back legs, or twin serpents
Where Purva Bhadrapada burns, Uttara Bhadrapada settles — deep, restrained, and still, like the serpent coiled at the bottom of the cosmic ocean.
Wisdom that comes from patience and depth rather than intensity; quiet endurance more than dramatic transformation.
Pushan (nourisher and protector of travelers and livestock)
A fish, or a drum
The zodiac's final nakshatra, and it plays the part: safe arrival, gentle completion, and a nourishing, protective quality especially toward those still in transit — literally Pushan's own domain.
A soft landing after everything Ashwini through Uttara Bhadrapada has moved through.

7th Lord in a Dusthana House

The lord of the 7th house (marriage/partnership) sitting in a dusthana (6th - conflict, 8th - upheaval/secrets, or 12th - loss/distance) is classically read as putting some strain on how easily partnership themes play out - not a specific behavior, just a harder road for the house's own significations to express smoothly.
7th Lord Conjunct a Natural Malefic

When a natural malefic (Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rahu, or Ketu) shares a house with the 7th lord, classical texts read it as coloring partnership themes with that malefic's own nature - conflict (Mars), ego friction (Sun), distance or delay (Saturn), restlessness or unconventional pulls (Rahu), or detachment (Ketu).
7th Lord Aspected by a Natural Malefic

A natural malefic aspecting (rather than sitting with) the 7th lord has a similar but generally milder classical reading than a direct conjunction - added pressure on partnership themes from that planet's own nature.
Venus-Mars Conjunction

Venus (romantic attraction, pleasure) conjunct Mars (desire, drive) is one of the more commonly discussed combinations in this area of classical astrology - read as intensified romantic/physical attraction, which some traditions associate with passionate, easily-formed bonds and others with restlessness around exclusivity.
Context (which houses, which signs, other aspects) matters more than the conjunction alone.
Venus-Mars Mutual Aspect

Venus and Mars aspecting each other without conjunction carries a related but generally softer version of the same themes as a direct Venus-Mars conjunction: intensified romantic/physical attraction, with the same range of classical readings.
Rahu Conjunct Venus

Rahu conjunct Venus is specifically and frequently cited in classical and popular sources discussing unconventional romantic patterns, amplified desire, or restlessness with convention in relationships - Rahu tends to exaggerate and destabilize whatever it touches, and Venus governs love and attraction.
Rahu in the 7th House

Rahu in the 7th house is read as bringing its own restless, boundary-pushing, amplifying nature directly into the partnership house - sometimes associated with unconventional relationship patterns, a strong pull toward partnership itself, or difficulty with settled convention.
Crowded 7th House

A 7th house with several planets in it is classically read as an area of life carrying a lot of weight and complexity - partnership themes are prominent and eventful, for better or worse depending on which planets are present and their own dignity.
Afflicted Venus

Venus debilitated or combust is read as the native's own relationship to romance, pleasure, and values being less settled or confident than usual - sometimes showing as difficulty knowing what one actually wants in a relationship, rather than pointing at any particular behavior.

A retrograde Mars often reads as drive and assertiveness turned inward rather than outward - action that's more deliberated, sometimes delayed or second-guessed, rather than the direct, immediate expression Mars usually shows.
Frustration can build when that inward-turned energy has no outlet, then release in a sudden burst.

A retrograde Mercury (the most commonly discussed retrograde placement, since Mercury retrogrades several times a year) often shows as a more internal, reflective communication and thinking style - reviewing, revising, and reconsidering rather than communicating in a first draft.
Some classical readings note a tendency to relearn or circle back to earlier ideas.
A retrograde Jupiter can turn its usual outward optimism and growth-seeking inward - wisdom and philosophy pursued more introspectively than through external teachers or conventional paths.
Some texts read it as delaying Jupiter's beneficial results until later in life, or requiring the native to find their own path to them rather than being handed one.

A retrograde Venus often shows as a more internally-defined, sometimes unconventional relationship to love, beauty, and pleasure - values and tastes worked out independently rather than absorbed from convention.
Some classical readings associate it with revisiting past relationships or reconsidering what's actually valued, rather than accepting inherited preferences.

A retrograde Saturn is, in several classical traditions, read as actually STRENGTHENING Saturn's own significations (discipline, structure, karmic lessons) rather than weakening them - an intensified, more internally-driven relationship to responsibility and delayed reward.
This is one of the more debated retrograde effects across sources; some texts simply treat it as a variant expression rather than a strengthening.
The same sign in both Rasi and Navamsa amplifies and stabilizes a planet's results, for better or worse.

When the Sun is debilitated, combust, or heavily afflicted, this period can instead bring ego conflicts, friction with authority figures or the father, setbacks to status or reputation, and health concerns connected to vitality, the heart, or bones.
A Moon mahadasha emphasizes the mind, emotions, the mother, domestic life, public perception, and matters requiring adaptability.
Because the Moon changes phase and sign quickly, this period's tone can vary noticeably depending on the Moon's strength at birth and by transit.

When the Moon is strong (waxing, exalted, in its own sign, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period tends to bring emotional stability, public popularity, domestic happiness, and success in fields involving the public, hospitality, or care-giving.

When the Moon is weak (waning, debilitated, or afflicted), this period can bring emotional instability, anxiety, fluctuating health (particularly fluid-related), and difficulties connected to the mother or domestic peace.
A Mars mahadasha brings heightened energy, courage, and drive, typically activating matters of property, siblings, technical or competitive pursuits, and assertive action.
This period often marks a phase of decisive initiative in the native's life.

When Mars is well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period favors achievement through bold, direct action, gains in property or land, success in technical, athletic, or competitive fields, and courageous leadership.
When Mars is debilitated or heavily afflicted, this period can bring conflict, disputes, accidents or injuries, impulsive decisions, and friction with siblings or through legal/property matters.

A Mercury mahadasha, being one of the longer periods, tends to shape a substantial phase of intellectual, communicative, and commercial development — emphasizing education, business, analytical work, and versatile skill-building.

When Mercury is well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period favors success in trade, writing, education, or analytical professions, sharp intellect, and effective, persuasive communication.
When Mercury is debilitated, combust, or heavily afflicted, this period can bring nervous anxiety, communication misunderstandings, indecisiveness, and setbacks in business or academic matters.

A Jupiter mahadasha, also a long period, generally emphasizes expansion, wisdom, ethical and spiritual growth, higher education, and overall good fortune, often marking a phase of significant life development.

When Jupiter is well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period tends to bring prosperity, respect, favorable developments regarding education, and marked spiritual or philosophical growth.
When Jupiter is debilitated or heavily afflicted, this period can bring overconfidence, excess, misplaced idealism, or delays in the growth and opportunities the native expects.
A Venus mahadasha, the longest of the nine, tends to define a major phase of life centered on relationships, marriage, comfort, artistic or aesthetic pursuits, and material prosperity.

When Venus is well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period favors happy relationships or marriage, material comfort and luxury, success in artistic, creative, or luxury-related fields, and general enjoyment of life.

When Venus is debilitated or heavily afflicted, this period can bring relationship discord, overindulgence, financial extravagance, and health concerns connected to the reproductive or urinary systems.
A Saturn mahadasha, the second-longest period, generally brings discipline, hard work, karmic lessons, and long-term structural change, often requiring patience before results become visible.

When Saturn is well-dignified (own sign, exalted, or otherwise well placed and unafflicted), this period rewards sustained, disciplined effort with steady, long-term achievement and authority earned through patience and responsibility.

When Saturn is debilitated or heavily afflicted, this period can bring prolonged hardship, health concerns, isolation, and financial struggle, with delays that may not resolve favorably without other mitigating factors in the chart.
A Rahu mahadasha typically brings unconventional ambition, sudden changes, intensified material desire, and often a connection to foreign lands, technology, or unconventional paths to status.

When Rahu is favorably placed (in a supportive house, not heavily afflicted, and well-disposed by its sign lord), this period can bring unconventional but substantial success, sudden rises in career or status, and gains connected to foreign or innovative ventures.

When Rahu is poorly placed or heavily afflicted, this period can bring confusion, obsession, scandal, instability, or anxiety, particularly regarding the specific life area (house) Rahu occupies and rules.

A Ketu mahadasha typically brings detachment, introspection, and a turning away from material focus in whichever life area Ketu occupies, often accompanied by heightened intuition or a spiritual/psychic dimension to experience.

When Ketu is favorably placed, this period can bring genuine spiritual growth, liberation from unhelpful attachments, and valuable, sometimes unexpected, intuitive insight or past-life talent surfacing.
When Ketu is poorly placed or heavily afflicted, this period can bring isolation, confusion, sudden and hard-to-explain losses, and health concerns connected to vitality or the nervous system.
